name: Yuputhimri
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Pama-Nyungan variety; Glottolog lists only Crowley 1981 subclassification note, no descriptive material.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1907. Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. III: Linguistics. Cambridge: University Press. pp.267ff. (sketch of Koko-Yimidir and Nggerikudi 'abbreviated from' NQE Bulletins 2 and 6).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Second-hand from Hey 1903; the 'Phonology' paragraph only explains the transcription alphabet; no accent/stress remark for Nggerikudi.

sources.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1981. The Mpakwithi dialect of Anguthimri. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 2, 146-194. Canberra: ANU Press. (ANU open-access scan hdl:1885/114846)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.149 sect. 1.3(iv) identifies the yupungati ('Nggerikudi' of Hey, 'yupngayt' to the Linngithigh) as speakers of Yuputhimri, 'closely related' to Anguthimri, lexicostatistics 60.0%; gives no Yuputhimri data. The stress statement pp.155-156 sect. 2.3 ('the first syllable and every alternate syllable receives stress.. if an otherwise stressable syllable is the last of a word, it is not stressed') is for Anguthimri (Mpakwithi dialect, angu1242) only.

sources.citation: O'Grady, G.N., C.F. Voegelin & F.M. Voegelin. 1966. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific fascicle six. Anthropological Linguistics 8(2):1-197 (Northern Paman section based on K. Hale's data).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.165: 'the Nggerikudi, alias Yupngayt, described by Hey who rightly regarded all of the dialects spoken along the coastline extending from Cullen Pt. to the northern side of Duyfken Point.. as belonging to the same language' (grouped with the Awngthim dialects). pp.167-168: comparative remark that in Northern Paman generally initial-syllable reduction is associated with 'a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable' -- historical/general, no synchronic statement for Yupngayth/Nggerikudi.

sources.citation: Hey, Rev. N. 1903. An elementary grammar of the Nggerikudi language (revised and edited by W.E. Roth). North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin No. 6. Brisbane: G.A. Vaughan, Government Printer. 23 pp. [in the bound UMich volume 'North Queensland Ethnography, Bulletins 1-8', Google scan on archive.org item northqueensland00landgoog, PDF pp.236-258]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent. No pronunciation or phonology section (sections 1-32 run from 'The Nggerikudi language' and noun lists through verbs, adverbs, interrogation, exclamations, songs); Preface only says spelling follows the RGS 'Orthography of Geographical Names'; no accent marks on any word. The only prosodic remarks are sentence-level: p.22 sect. 30 'Interrogation is usually expressed by the tone of the voice' and p.23 sect. 31 'Note: Anger and intensity are expressed by prolonging the last syllable in the sentence.'

sources.note: Names/codes only (Nggerikudi = Yupungati/Yuputhimri; AIATSIS Y19 Yupangathi); vowel chart is Anguthimri from Lynch 1998; nothing on stress.
